prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision measurement.

statement.case_for: I moved my own first-place ballot, the IceCube candidate B025, down in favour of the optical lattice clock candidate B046, which I had at rank 3. B046 is the only candidate that five of eight members placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with quite different tastes: Kroll and Lindroth rank it first, Johansson and Olsson second. As an instrument builder I judge it on the criteria I care most about. The magic-wavelength proposal by Katori, followed by the strontium lattice clock, is a concept that was turned into a device with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The performance has been reproduced and compared independently at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others, so the systematics have been tested by people who did not build the original apparatus. It opens new measurements (relativistic redshift over millimetre scales, tests of constants, dark-matter searches), so it is more than an incremental improvement. The credit is also unusually clean: two named people, one holding the concept and first demonstration, the other the record accuracy and many-body clock work. A two-person prize for a verified, mature measurement advance is something the committee can defend without a long attribution argument.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, quantum control of ions) already cover neighbouring metrology, and Ye is intimately connected to the comb work, so a sceptic can say this repeats a theme. A second concern is that the optical clock community also includes ion-clock groups and Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, and a two-name prize leaves a visible gap. A third is timing: the SI redefinition of the second is still pending, and some would wait for it. None of these seems decisive to me, since the invention is distinct from the comb and from ion control, but I cannot verify the detailed priority history from the supplied material.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as an instrument that changes what can be measured, and notes that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes could be read as dilution and that Lemonde or Ludlow might deserve a share.
responses.response: I agree on the instrument argument and I share it. On dilution I would be firm: the comb gave a frequency ruler and the ion work gave control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a different invention, because magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at once and that is what brings the statistical power to 1e-18. On Lemonde and Ludlow I am less sure than you are that a third name is needed, because the three-person cap would force us to choose and the Katori and Ye pair carries the concept and the performance record. I would still want the citation worded narrowly enough to avoid implying that Katori and Ye alone built every clock.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B006) first as the architecture of superconducting quantum processors and the natural successor to the 2025 prize, and says she knows the field closely but has professional proximity to the community.
responses.response: I take your expertise seriously, and I accept that circuit QED is scientifically strong and well confirmed. My difficulty is twofold. First, the credit is genuinely unresolved: four names are credited, you and Kroll propose different trios (Girvin against Blais), and the proposal and first strong-coupling demonstration are intertwined, so we would be deciding between collaborators in an argument that is not settled. Second, following a 2025 prize for superconducting circuits with another circuit prize in 2026 risks looking like a single community being rewarded twice in a row, and you yourself flag the closeness to Devoret. I would not rule B006 out for a later year, but at present B046 has the cleaner attribution and broader support, and your flagged proximity is a reason for care in how much weight the committee gives your ranking.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks WMAP first and my IceCube candidate B025 sixth, doubting that a single credited name for IceCube is fair for a large collaboration and a long-developed detector concept, and noting that individual source identification is still limited.
responses.response: That is a fair criticism and it is the main reason I have dropped B025 from first place. I put Halzen first because the detection of the diffuse astrophysical flux, then the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 results and the Galactic-plane map, opened a new window, and I still think the discovery is real. But a sole prize to Halzen leaves out the earlier AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers and the collaboration leadership, and I cannot settle that from what we have. I would keep B025 as a serious alternative if the committee can find a defensible two or three name credit, but I will not argue for it as it stands. On WMAP I do not share your confidence: COBE (2006) and the 2019 cosmology prize cover much of the same ground, and I do not see a decisive step beyond them.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B038) first as a verified theory-to-experiment chain, but accepts that credit for the HgTe proposal and for the 3D topological insulator lies partly outside the three supplied names.
responses.response: I do not have the expertise to judge B038 against the condensed-matter alternatives, so I rely on you and on Olsson, who also ranks it first. What I can say is that it did not make my own ballot, which says more about my field than about the candidate. The attribution is my concern: Kane and Mele are clear, but you, Lindroth and Johansson all point to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and to the 3D discoveries, and a prize that omits those will be criticised. If you can argue that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp give a coherent citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect, I would support B038 as the second part of a two-part prize or as the preferred choice if B046 stalls.

uncertainties: Whether a lattice clock prize is judged too close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether a third name (Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow) is needed.
Whether the committee should wait for the SI redefinition of the second, or treat the pending redefinition as a reason to act now.
Whether B025 can be given a fair multi-person credit that covers the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers and the IceCube leadership, since a sole Halzen prize looks fragile.
Whether B038 or B006 would draw stronger committee support once the attribution problems are discussed by the specialists, as I cannot judge either independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B046, which is atomic and metrology physics outside my own collaborations. For B025 I should note that I am an astroparticle physicist and work in neighbouring cosmic-ray and gamma-ray collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), so I have professional proximity to the IceCube community, although no personal or institutional tie to the credited person is stated in my profile.
